Empirical Research Plan: “Do Merger Waves Propagate through Supply-Chain Links?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Exposure-weighted Difference-in-Differences (a Bartik/shift-share design
estimated in an event-study framework).

Rationale  
• We observe repeated “treatments’’ (industry merger waves) that start at
different times (1986–2010).  
• Industries differ ex-ante in the intensity of their buyer–supplier ties to
any other industry; this time-invariant input-output matrix provides the
shift-share weights.  
• After an origin industry j enters a wave, a linked industry i experiences a
plausibly exogenous increase in “exposure’’ to that wave equal to
Link_{ij} × Wave_{j,t}.  
• The panel (industry i × year t) allows us to difference out permanent
industry factors (γ_i) and economy-wide shocks (δ_t).  
• The design is analogous to Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2013) China-exposure
DID and uses the recent Sun & Abraham (2021) / Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021)
estimators to handle staggered adoption and dynamic effects.

Estimand of interest  
β: the causal effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure to
customer/supplier wave activity on the number (or log dollar value) of mergers
undertaken by industry i.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Panel unit: 4-digit SIC industry-year.

Treatment variable  
Exposure_i,t ≡ Σ_j  Link_{ij} × Wave_{j,t−1}  
• Link_{ij}: 1982 BEA input-output flow from j to i (customer) or i to j
(supplier), scaled so Σ_j Link_{ij}=1.  
• Wave_{j,t} = 1 if industry j is in a merger wave year per Harford (2005),
0 otherwise.

Interpretation: high Exposure_i,t industries are “treated’’ in years when their
major trading partners have just entered a wave.

Control group  
Industry-years with zero (or very low, e.g., bottom quartile) Exposure in year
t form the counterfactual. These industries face the same macro shocks but are
only weakly linked to wave origins.

Timing  
Year t is the first full calendar year after the origin industry’s wave start
date; we also estimate dynamic leads/lags k = –3,…,+5.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends conditional on fixed effects.  
Absent customer/supplier waves, merger activity trends would be parallel across
industries with high vs. low Link weights.

Plausibility: The IO matrix is measured years before most waves, so link
strength is predetermined. Including γ_i and δ_t, plus controls for own-industry
conditions (Tobin’s Q, credit conditions), makes A1 plausible but untestable.

A2. No anticipatory treatment effects.  
Linked industries cannot perfectly foresee an upcoming wave in customers and
revise their own M&A behavior before t –1.

Plausibility: Difficult for suppliers to forecast aggregate wave onsets; we can
empirically test for pre-trends (event-study leads).

A3. Exogeneity of link matrix.  
The geographic/technological pattern of trade flows is not chosen in response
to future merger waves (fixed long before the sample period).

Plausibility: We use the 1982 IO table throughout; robustness with 1977 and
1992 tables supports exogeneity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Common shocks that affect both origin and linked industries (e.g.,
technology).  
Remedy: Include origin-industry–year controls interacted with Link_{ij}
(“leave-one-out control”), and 2-digit-year fixed effects.

T2. Reverse causality: i’s own merger wave may induce mergers in j, not vice
versa (simultaneity).  
Remedy: Lag exposure (use t–1, t–2 averages); instrument Wave_{j,t} with
regulatory shocks specific to j (e.g., deregulation dummies) in a 2SLS version.

T3. Heterogeneous staggered adoption bias.  
Remedy: Estimate event-study using Sun & Abraham (2021) att_gt() and
aggregate_to_att() functions; never-treated and not-yet-treated act as
appropriate controls.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# install.packages(c("data.table","fixest","did","sandwich","lmtest"))
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(did); library(lmtest)

#-----------------------------
# 1. Load & merge data
#-----------------------------
mna  <- fread("sdc_deals.csv")        # deal-level
crsp <- fread("crsp_returns.csv")
io   <- fread("bea_io_1982.csv")      # i = buyer(row), j = seller(col)
waves<- fread("industry_waves.csv")   # Harford indicator at 4-digit-year level
comp <- fread("compustat_funda.csv")

#-----------------------------
# 2. Construct industry-year M&A counts
#-----------------------------
# keep completed US acquisitions >$1m
mna <- mna[Value > 1 & Nation=="USA"]
mna[, year := year(DealDate)]
mna_ind <- mna[, .(MNA_Count=.N, MNA_Value=sum(Value)),
               by=.(AcqSIC4=substr(AcquirerSIC,1,4), year)]

#-----------------------------
# 3. Exposure variable
#-----------------------------
# reshape IO so Link_ij sums to 1 within i
io_melt <- melt(io, id.vars="buyer_sic4",
                variable.name="seller_sic4", value.name="flow")
io_melt[, Link := flow / sum(flow), by=buyer_sic4]
setnames(io_melt, c("buyer_sic4","seller_sic4"), c("i_sic4","j_sic4"))

# merge wave status of origin industries
waves[, Wave := 1]           # Wave==1 else NA will be filled by 0 later
waves <- waves[,
        .(j_sic4   = sic4,
          year,
          Wave = Wave)]
# create full grid of (i,year)
yrs  <- 1986:2010
ind  <- unique(io_melt$i_sic4)
grid <- CJ(i_sic4=ind, year=yrs)

# compute exposure_i,t = sum_j Link_ij * Wave_j,t-1
expo <- merge(io_melt, waves, by=c("j_sic4"), allow.cartesian=TRUE)
expo[, year := year]                       # waves’ own year
expo[, Wave := fifelse(is.na(Wave),0,Wave)]
expo[, year := year +1]                    # t-1 lag
expo_agg <- expo[, .(Exposure = sum(Link*Wave)), by=.(i_sic4, year)]

#-----------------------------
# 4. Final analysis dataset
#-----------------------------
panel <- merge(grid, expo_agg, by=c("i_sic4","year"), all.x=TRUE)
panel[is.na(Exposure), Exposure:=0]

panel <- merge(panel, mna_ind,
               by.x=c("i_sic4","year"),
               by.y=c("AcqSIC4","year"), all.x=TRUE)
panel[is.na(MNA_Count),  MNA_Count := 0]

# industry & year fixed effects identifiers
panel[, ind_fe := i_sic4]
panel[, yr_fe  := year]

#-----------------------------
# 5. Main regression
#-----------------------------
est <- feols(MNA_Count ~ Exposure | ind_fe + yr_fe, data=panel,
             vcov = ~ind_fe + yr_fe)        # two-way clustering
summary(est)

#-----------------------------
# 6. Event-study (Sun & Abraham)
#-----------------------------
# Define first treatment year for each industry
panel[, treated := as.integer(Exposure>0)]
panel[, first_treat := ifelse(treated==1, min(year), NA),
      by=ind_fe]
did_dat <- as.data.frame(panel)   # package 'did' needs data.frame

es <- att_gt(yname="MNA_Count",
             tname="year",
             idname="ind_fe",
             gname="first_treat",
             data = did_dat,
             xformla = ~1,
             clustervars="ind_fe")

es_agg <- aggte(es, type="dynamic")
summary(es_agg)
ggdid(es_agg)

#-----------------------------
# 7. Robustness: alternative IO weight (1977 table)
#-----------------------------
io77  <- fread("bea_io_1977.csv")
# (repeat Link construction, replace Exposure, re-estimate)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prediction: β > 0. A one-sd increase in Exposure (≈ 0.08) raises the number of
deals in the linked industry by roughly 10–15 %.  
Intuition: Supplier consolidation mitigates increased bargaining risk created
by a buyer wave; positive abnormal returns for suppliers’ acquirers will be
larger when customer waves were value-increasing (positive origin CARs).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/Bartik)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-trend/parallel trend evidence (lead coefficients ≈ 0) ........ 1  
C2: No differential time-varying confounders after controlling FE ..... 0.5  
C3: Stable unit treatment value (limited cross-industry interference) . 0.5  
C4: Proper treatment timing (exposure uses lagged Wave) .............. 1  
C5: Robustness to alternative weights / instruments .................. 1  
Total (out of 5) ..................................................... 4.0
